theme: Gog and Magog, God’s ultimate protection
readingInstruction: Read Ezekiel 38:1-39:29. A great invasion by Gog of Magog is described, and God defeats it. These chapters are hard to interpret, so read for the main point: God protects his restored people, and the nations will know he is the LORD.
settingTheScene: After the restoration promises of chapters 33 to 37, these chapters describe a final attack on God’s people. Gog, the chief prince of Meshech and Tubal, comes with a coalition of nations from the far north against a people living securely in unwalled villages. The name Gog does not match any known historical king. Interpreters understand the passage in different ways: as a symbol of the final assault against God’s people, as a prediction of a particular event, or as apocalyptic imagery. All agree on its main point.
observation: “Son of man, set your face toward Gog, of the land of Magog, the chief prince of Meshech and Tubal” (38:2).
“I will turn you about and put hooks into your jaws” (38:4).
“After many days you will be mustered. In the latter years you will go against the land that has been restored from war” (38:8).
“You will say, I will go up against the land of unwalled villages” (38:11).
“I will show my greatness and my holiness and make myself known in the eyes of many nations” (38:23).
“I will give to Gog a place for burial in Israel” (39:11).
“And the house of Israel shall know that I am the LORD their God, from that day forward” (39:22).
“And I will not hide my face anymore from them, when I pour out my Spirit upon the house of Israel” (39:29).
interpretation:
The attack comes at a time of peace. The people are dwelling securely, apparently defenseless. Gog’s plan is to seize plunder. But God says, “I will turn you about and put hooks into your jaws.” Though Gog thinks he is acting by his own will, God is leading him out. The invasion is under God’s control, and its purpose is to display God’s greatness.

The defeat is dramatic: an earthquake, a plague, torrential rain, hailstones, fire and sulfur. The invading armies turn on each other. Their weapons are so numerous that Israel will burn them for seven years. The bodies are buried in a valley, and it takes seven months to clear the land. All of this serves the aim: “I will make myself known in the eyes of many nations. Then they will know that I am the LORD.”

The big question is how to understand this. Some interpret it as a literal battle in the end times. Others see in it a symbol of the continuing assault of the powers of this world against God’s people, which ends with God’s victory. Revelation 20:7-9 takes up the names Gog and Magog for the final rebellion of the nations after the thousand years, and says fire comes down from heaven and consumes them. In this use, Gog and Magog stand for the last desperate attack on God’s people. Whatever the details, the point is that God has the last word.

The conclusion in chapter 39 is a reminder of why the exile happened and a promise: “The nations shall know that the house of Israel went into captivity for their iniquity.” But now God will restore their fortunes, “and I will not hide my face anymore from them, when I pour out my Spirit upon the house of Israel.” The final note is the Spirit. The people who were scattered will be gathered and filled.
connection: Revelation 20:7-10 describes the last rebellion of the nations, “Gog and Magog,” and their defeat by fire from heaven. Revelation 19:17-21 pictures the great supper of God, echoing Ezekiel 39:17-20. Joel 2:28-29 and Acts 2:16-18 speak of the pouring out of the Spirit. Romans 8:31 asks, “If God is for us, who can be against us?” Psalm 2 shows the nations raging and the LORD laughing in heaven. Matthew 16:18 says the gates of hell will not prevail.
application:
Whatever happens in the world, remember that God has the last word.

Do not let fear of the future overshadow your trust in the God who protects his people.

Pray that the Spirit would be poured out on your church and on the people of God worldwide.
prayerPrompts: Tell God what you fear from the enemies of his people.
Thank him that he is sovereign over every nation.
Ask him for confidence in the end.
